strings.name: Joshua Wong
strings.role: Hong Kong democracy activist and co-founder of Demosisto
strings.summary: Joshua Wong helped found Scholarism while at secondary school and became known for opposing national education proposals and participating in the 2014 Umbrella Movement. He later co-founded Demosisto. His political advocacy, international lobbying and multiple court cases remain contentious. He was still imprisoned in November 2026; the latest national security case reached sentencing on 5 November.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026, including reports of his actual court appearance and sentencing on 5 November. Pleas, convictions, sentences and appeals in different cases are distinguished. Overturning a sentence is not acquittal, and no release date is independently calculated.
strings.influence.rationale: Participated in Hong Kong's student and democracy movements; his political activities and legal experiences have sustained international attention to civil rights.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and early involvement
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Hong Kong on 13 October 1996. While still at secondary school in 2011, he organised Scholarism with others to campaign over the proposed Moral and National Education curriculum.
strings.facts.f2.label: Organisational background
strings.facts.f2.value: Scholarism and Demosisto were separate organisations. He co-founded Demosisto with Nathan Law and others in 2016. It announced its dissolution on 30 June 2020 and should not be presented as an organisation in which he currently holds an active office.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Student mobilisation and international advocacy
strings.highlights.h1.text: His activities expanded from school-curriculum disputes to electoral arrangements, street protests and international lobbying. The Umbrella Movement involved multiple organisations and participants; he was one of its internationally prominent figures, rather than the sole leader or source of its achievements.
strings.highlights.h2.title: National security cases and rights disputes
strings.highlights.h2.text: Hong Kong's government says the 2026 sentence safeguards national security. Human Rights Watch criticises the prosecution and lengthy sentence as harming freedom of expression and calls for his release. Judicial outcomes are presented separately from these political and rights assessments; a guilty plea does not erase debates over the law and its enforcement.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Sentenced to ten years in another national security case
strings.timeline.t1.text: After pleading guilty on 2 September to conspiracy to collude with foreign countries or external elements to endanger national security, he received a ten-year sentence. RTHK reported that two months and two days would run concurrently with his existing sentence in another case. The terms cannot simply be added together or the previous expected release date retained.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Faces a new collusion charge while imprisoned
strings.timeline.t2.text: Appeared at West Kowloon Magistrates' Courts on a new conspiracy-to-collude charge concerning requests for foreign sanctions and related conduct between 1 July and 23 November 2020. This was the charging stage of a new case; the guilty plea and sentence followed in 2026. It is separate from the primary-election case.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Receives a 56-month sentence in the primary-election case
strings.timeline.t3.text: After pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion in a case involving the unofficial 2020 Legislative Council primary, he was sentenced to four years and eight months. The sentencing reasons classified him as an active participant and reduced the term for his plea. This sentence is distinct from the later collusion case.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Demosisto announces dissolution
strings.timeline.t4.text: The organisation announced its dissolution on the day the NPC Standing Committee passed the Hong Kong National Security Law. His 2016 co-founder status should not be treated as a current office in an operating organisation. Subsequent assembly and national security cases are addressed separately.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Sentence appeal succeeds in the Civic Square case
strings.timeline.t5.text: The Court of Final Appeal set aside the prison term imposed on sentence review in 2017 and reinstated Wong's original 80-hour community-service order. The ruling concerned punishment, not reversal of his conviction, and did not cover his separate contempt case over the Mong Kok protest-site clearance.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Co-founds Demosisto
strings.timeline.t6.text: Launched Demosisto with Nathan Law and others, extending student activism into political organisation, elections and international advocacy. Law was the founding chair; their roles should not be confused.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Participates in the Civic Square action
strings.timeline.t7.text: Took part in entering the government headquarters forecourt, the incident underlying his later unlawful-assembly case. It occurred as the Umbrella Movement was emerging. Conduct in the particular case, the wider movement and its different participants should be distinguished.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Helps found Scholarism
strings.timeline.t8.text: In a 2015 interview, he said he and others formed Scholarism in May 2011 to oppose the proposed Moral and National Education curriculum. In September 2012, the government removed the three-year implementation deadline and left decisions to schools. This was not a permanent abolition of all national education.
